spec.topic: Should national elections use proportional representation instead of single-member constituencies?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: National elections should use proportional representation instead of single-member constituencies. The main reason is that under the current system millions of votes go to losing candidates and count for nothing.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A party can take a large majority of seats with well under half of the national vote. That matters, since a government elected on a minority of votes lacks a clear democratic mandate, which is why the system should change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Critics say proportional systems often produce coalition governments that are unstable.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: But several countries with proportional representation have had stable coalitions lasting many years.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Constituency MPs do have a personal link to a local area, and proportional lists would weaken it.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Still, mixed systems can keep local representatives while matching seats to votes.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: I once lived in a constituency where one party won every election for forty years.

spec.topic: Should youth football leagues prohibit heading the ball until players reach sixteen?

utterances.speaker: Dimitri
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether youth football leagues should prohibit heading until players reach sixteen. Leopold supports the proposal, while Renata opposes it.

utterances.speaker: Leopold

utterances.speaker: Renata

spec.topic: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether every serious criminal offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, why do you support that rule?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Serious criminal offences should require unanimous jury verdicts. A unanimous verdict better protects defendants from wrongful conviction.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: That protection matters because requiring every juror to agree forces doubts about weak evidence into the discussion.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Yara, do you think unanimity is necessary?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: A non-unanimous verdict can still be fair when the evidence strongly favours guilt.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: But a non-unanimous verdict can convict someone even when several jurors retain reasonable doubt. For context, Yara has observed jury selection in two serious trials.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Unanimity is an important safeguard against unreliable convictions. The jury system also differs considerably between jurisdictions.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: In other words, Magnus regards unanimity as protection against unreliable convictions.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: So you are saying that unanimity protects defendants by requiring complete jury agreement.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Put another way, the argument is that a serious conviction should not stand without full jury agreement. Seamus, what is your strongest reason for a demanding standard?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Serious offences can result in lifelong imprisonment, and therefore the law should demand the highest level of jury agreement for those offences.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Jurors receive detailed instructions about the burden of proof in serious cases, so those instructions give jurors a clear basis for refusing to agree when the prosecution has not proved its case.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Appeal courts can review serious convictions when legal errors may have affected the verdict; that is why some critics believe unanimous verdicts are not the only protection against injustice.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has highlighted both the protection offered by unanimity and the safeguards that exist when jurors disagree. The debate is being broadcast during the evening news programme.

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Chidi

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: I once served on a jury that deliberated for three days. I am not claiming that experience settles the legal question.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Still, a unanimous-verdict requirement can prolong deliberations, especially when the evidence is complicated.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: A related concern is what happens after disagreement. When a jury cannot agree, the court often has to arrange a retrial.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Exactly, and retrials consume victims' time and public money. That is why some people prefer a qualified majority.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: A majority verdict can resolve a trial even when one juror remains unconvinced. In that sense, it avoids making one dissent decisive.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: That would reduce the number of hung trials, although it would not remove every risk of a mistaken conviction.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Because that finding is shared by every juror, a verdict accepted by every juror has greater legitimacy. The public is more likely to trust a decision that no juror rejects.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our final question is whether that legitimacy should determine the rule. On balance, the law should require unanimous verdicts for every serious offence.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Tonight we are asking whether eligible citizens should be required to vote, with a modest penalty for unjustified abstention. Lorenzo, why support the policy?

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would turn participation into a legal duty. Because a legal duty signals that elections are a shared civic responsibility, it would give voting a clearer public meaning.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Zainab, is that civic argument persuasive?

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Not entirely. Compulsory voting could make citizens feel coerced rather than represented, but I accept that participation matters.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: What safeguards would make a penalty acceptable?

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: Illness and emergencies can prevent eligible citizens from voting. A system that ignores those circumstances would be unfair.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: That is why accessible exemptions would protect citizens prevented from voting by illness or emergencies.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: So you are saying that a humane penalty system depends on usable exemptions for people who cannot vote.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Abena, would a modest penalty actually change behaviour?

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: A modest penalty would give occasional nonvoters a reason to make voting routine. Therefore, compulsory voting would raise turnout.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: In other words, the proposal seeks broader participation by making abstention costly.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: That is another reason to support the policy: the penalty would preserve free choice among candidates while discouraging abstention.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: For my part, I have voted in every national election since turning eighteen.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Meera, what remains unresolved?

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: The proposed penalty has not yet been specified in currency. We should settle that detail before judging whether it is genuinely modest.

utterances.speaker: Annelise

spec.topic: Should businesses replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave?

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Businesses should replace fixed holiday allowances with unlimited paid leave, provided the policy includes clear safeguards. The change is not a licence to deny holidays; it is a different way to organise them.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Unlimited paid leave gives employees more control over when they take time off, which is a strong reason to prefer it to a rigid allowance.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A flexible leave policy can help employees manage illness, caring duties, and unexpected personal needs. That practical flexibility is another reason for the change.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: However, unlimited paid leave can lead some employees to take fewer holidays than they would under a fixed allowance. The author has worked in both open-plan and private offices.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In other words, businesses should adopt unlimited leave with protections rather than treat leave as an informal privilege.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Unlimited leave can remove the annual rush to use days before they expire, so it can make time off feel less like a vanishing benefit.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A well-designed unlimited-leave policy can signal that employers value results and wellbeing more than attendance, which offers a further case for replacing fixed allowances.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: The author keeps a paper calendar beside the computer.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: A monitored pilot can show whether unlimited leave changes staffing levels, output, or employees’ actual time off, because those measures expose problems that slogans would conceal.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: For that reason, a monitored trial is a sensible first step for a business considering unlimited paid leave.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: Put another way, unlimited leave is worthwhile when it combines employee freedom with enforceable minimum standards.

utterances.speaker: Author
utterances.text: In short, businesses should replace fixed allowances with safeguarded unlimited paid leave.

spec.topic: Should amateur boxing replace winning by knockout with points-only scoring?

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: I think amateur boxing should replace winning by knockout with points-only scoring. The aim should be to test skill without making one blow decisive.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would reduce the risk of serious head injuries, which is the strongest reason for the change.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Most amateur boxers have limited defensive experience because they are still developing their technique.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would also make bouts fairer when one lucky punch decides the result. That matters because a single dramatic moment can erase several rounds of better boxing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: A single punch can end a bout even when the other boxer has performed better overall.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Another benefit is that points-only scoring would encourage boxers to develop a wider range of skills.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: They would gain more from footwork, defence, and sustained combinations if judges scored the whole performance, so training would become less focused on finding one big punch.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Points-only scoring would make bouts less frightening for beginners, and that could help small clubs attract people.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Beginners may leave boxing when they see a teammate lose by a sudden knockout; for that reason, removing knockouts could protect participation.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Exactly, and points-only scoring would make it easier for clubs to retain new participants.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: A side note: the community gym has added new showers this month.

utterances.speaker: Constance
utterances.text: But removing knockout victories would make boxing less honest about the sport's physical risks. A knockout is dangerous, but it also makes that danger impossible to ignore.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: So you are saying that a points-only system would conceal rather than solve boxing's dangers.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: Put another way, Chloe's proposal would judge amateur boxers only on accumulated points instead of allowing a knockout to decide the bout.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Even so, points-only scoring would encourage a more patient style of amateur boxing.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: I have competed in three tournaments this year, although that experience does not settle the policy question.

utterances.speaker: Chloe
utterances.text: Constance's concern, as I understand it, is that a points-only system could hide the seriousness of a hard punch.

utterances.speaker: Darius
utterances.text: That concern is manageable because judges could still reward controlled pressure and accurate combinations under a points-only system.

utterances.text: Terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying, because dying people have the right to decide how much suffering they endure.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Palliative care cannot relieve all pain in every case, I grant that.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: But a legal right would pressure vulnerable patients to choose death, since elderly patients often worry about being a burden on their families.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Strict safeguards like two independent doctors and a waiting period can prevent that kind of pressure.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Doctors sometimes misjudge how long a patient has left, so patients could ask on the basis of a wrong prognosis.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: My sister nursed our father through his last illness, so I have seen this up close.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: But prognosis errors are rare when the limit is six months and two specialists confirm it.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Oregon is a good test, since assisted dying is legal there and the law has run for over two decades without widespread abuse.

utterances.speaker: Kai
utterances.text: Still, it would erode trust between doctors and patients, because doctors are meant to heal and not to kill.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: Doctors already accept refusals of life-saving treatment, so respecting a patient's wish about death is already part of medicine.

utterances.speaker: Kai

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: So you are saying that distinction matters, but honestly I find it thin in the final days of a life.

utterances.speaker: Joaquin
utterances.text: In other words, patients should have a legal option when suffering cannot be relieved.

spec.topic: Should criminal trials require unanimous jury verdicts in every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Our question is whether every serious criminal offence should require a unanimous jury verdict. Magnus, you support that rule.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: I do. Serious criminal offences should require unanimous verdicts because unanimity protects defendants when one juror retains a reasonable doubt.

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: That protection matters because a dissenting juror can identify overlooked evidence or a mistaken interpretation.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But unanimity also allows one holdout juror to block a verdict supported by the rest of the jury.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: That objection is especially strong because a single holdout can make a lengthy and complex trial impossible to resolve fairly.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: For context, I have served as a juror once. Lengthy trials can give one determined juror disproportionate leverage over the other jurors, which is another reason to worry about unanimity.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Seamus, do you favour a compromise rather than one rule for every serious offence?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Yes. Unanimous verdicts should be required only when a conviction could result in life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would preserve the strongest safeguard where an error is hardest to undo.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Our courts handle many serious trials involving digital evidence and financial records. But restricting unanimity to life-imprisonment cases would leave other serious offences without a unanimous verdict requirement.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, what would you use for those other offences?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Other serious offences should instead be decided by a two-thirds jury majority.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So Magnus is proposing a two-thirds majority for serious offences that do not carry life imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: Judges should explain publicly how a jury dealt with substantial dissent.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: In other words, Chidi's proposal is that judges should report how serious disagreements within the jury were handled.

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Every juror's unresolved doubt should be recorded before the jury announces its verdict.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus is calling for each juror's remaining doubt to be documented before a verdict is announced.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: The panel has therefore discussed unanimity, qualified majorities, and formal records of dissent rather than a single automatic rule.

utterances.speaker: Magnus

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Yara, what is your response?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: But a unanimity requirement lets one juror block a verdict even when the evidence persuades everyone else. That can turn a safeguard into an arbitrary veto.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, does unanimity have a wider benefit than protecting the defendant?

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: The jury room in Wanjiru's courthouse has twelve chairs, so the practical discussion can involve many different views.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Chidi, could a different voting threshold protect fairness?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: A supermajority can prevent one juror from causing a deadlock without removing the need for broad agreement. Therefore, serious offences should permit a ten-to-two verdict after genuine deliberation.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: You have worked around courts for years. Does that proposal reflect your experience?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: I have watched several jury selections during my legal career.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Seamus, what would a ten-to-two rule achieve?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: A ten-to-two verdict would still require substantial agreement among jurors, because it could protect defendants while reducing hung trials.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Magnus, your final argument for unanimity?

utterances.speaker: Magnus
utterances.text: Unanimous convictions make it harder for prosecutors to win cases based on weak evidence. That is why protection against weak convictions is a legitimate reason to retain unanimous verdicts.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: So, Yara, you are saying that the issue is not broad agreement but the power of one dissenting juror?

utterances.speaker: Yara

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Chidi, can you state the alternative plainly?

utterances.speaker: Chidi
utterances.text: A ten-to-two verdict would preserve broad agreement while avoiding a one-person veto.

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru

utterances.speaker: Wanjiru
utterances.text: Before we close, Seamus, what cost matters most when a jury cannot agree?

utterances.speaker: Seamus
utterances.text: Hung juries impose financial and emotional costs on courts and victims.

utterances.speaker: Yara
utterances.text: Put another way, Seamus's concern is that hung juries impose costs on courts and victims.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would raise participation in elections. That matters because governments should reflect more than the people who are already most engaged.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A penalty could unfairly burden eligible citizens whose transport or work arrangements make voting difficult. A modest fine is still serious for someone on a tight budget.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would give poorer citizens a stronger political voice. They are often the people least able to absorb the consequences of low turnout.

utterances.speaker: Meera
utterances.text: Compulsory voting would coerce citizens into expressing a political preference. I do not think the state should force political participation.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: Using the existing electoral register would make enforcement of a modest penalty manageable. The system would record non-attendance and allow people to submit a justification.

utterances.speaker: Zainab
utterances.text: A modest penalty would reduce habitual abstention. Some people skip elections simply because there is no immediate reason for them to attend.

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: The safeguards are crucial: exemptions for illness and caring duties would prevent many unfair fines. People should be able to challenge a penalty easily.

utterances.speaker: Annelise
utterances.text: Meera, does that answer your concern about coercion?

utterances.speaker: Abena
utterances.text: Put another way, you are saying that exemptions for illness and caring duties are necessary to avoid unfair fines. That should be written into the law rather than left to administrative discretion.

utterances.speaker: Lorenzo
utterances.text: The polling station in my district opens at seven o'clock on election day. Even so, the policy should focus on giving people a practical chance to vote, not simply issuing fines.

utterances.speaker: Gwen

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: What is the strongest reason for making the requirement universal?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: Water restrictions are becoming frequent in drought-prone districts. The difficulty is that rainwater-collection systems impose an upfront cost on new homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: So the cost is your main reservation?

utterances.speaker: Gwen
utterances.text: It is a reservation, but not a reason to reject the policy. Rainwater-collection systems can reduce stormwater runoff, and tanks can be installed beneath patios in many new homes.

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Gwen

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Gwen

utterances.speaker: Gwen

utterances.speaker: Interviewer
utterances.text: And is the proposal technically realistic for ordinary developments?

utterances.speaker: Gwen

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Interviewer

utterances.speaker: Gwen

spec.topic: Should managers be required to advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally?

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Our question tonight is whether managers should advertise internal candidates before recruiting externally. Bongani, make the case for the requirement.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates already understand the organisation's systems and culture. More importantly, employees deserve fair notice of opportunities to advance within their organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: External recruitment can bring skills that the organisation does not currently possess. Some specialist vacancies also attract very few qualified internal applicants.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: Rosalind raises the concern about restricting the search. Yusuf, what would an internal advertisement achieve?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Transparent internal advertising increases employees' trust in management. Employees are also more likely to apply for advancement when opportunities are clearly advertised.

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Internal candidates often require less organisational induction than external hires, which can make the appointment more efficient.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: For those reasons, especially fair notice, greater trust, wider participation, and lower induction costs, managers should be required to advertise vacancies internally before recruiting externally. The external applicants should still remain eligible after that internal advertisement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: That sounds like a sequence rather than a ban on outside applicants. Yusuf, can the process remain practical?

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: Yes, because an internal-first rule would preserve access to external talent. A short internal application window would also prevent the recruitment process from becoming unnecessarily slow.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So the proposed safeguard is a brief internal window, followed by a normal comparison of candidates?

utterances.speaker: Bongani
utterances.text: Exactly. Managers could compare internal and external applicants after the internal advertisement period. In other words, the proposal would open the door internally without shutting out outsiders.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: So, in summary, the proposal is a mandatory internal advertisement before any external search. Put another way, employees would receive fair notice before managers looked outside the organisation.

utterances.speaker: Rosalind
utterances.text: That is to say, the rule would preserve a fair chance for external applicants after internal notice. Separately, the company currently has twelve departments with separate recruitment budgets.

utterances.speaker: Yusuf
utterances.text: But a mandatory internal stage could delay urgent recruitment by at least a week, so I would oppose an inflexible requirement.

utterances.speaker: Hector
utterances.text: The disagreement is therefore about timing, not whether internal employees deserve visibility. We will move to closing statements.

utterances.text: Terminally ill patients should have the legal right to request assisted dying, because competent adults have authority over their own bodies. Besides, prolonging a death full of suffering serves no one's interest.
